title: Replication
subtitle: Single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless database replication topologies, WAL shipping, and failover mechanics.
keyTakeaways: Replication copies data across multiple physical machines to provide redundancy, failover protection, and read scaling.
Single-leader replication routes all writes through a primary node; asynchronous replication offers high write performance but risks data loss during ungraceful failover.
Multi-leader and leaderless topologies permit writes across multiple datacenters, but require conflict resolution mechanisms (LWW, vector clocks, or CRDTs).
architectureDiagram:
REPLICATION TOPOLOGIES
1. SINGLE-LEADER (Primary-Replica via WAL Streaming):
   [ App Writes ] -> [ Primary Node ] === Async WAL Streaming ===> [ Read Replica 1 ]
                                                              ===> [ Read Replica 2 ]

2. LEADERLESS QUORUM (Dynamo / Cassandra):
   [ App Writes ] --- Concurrent writes to N replicas ---> [ Replica A (Ack) ]
                                                      ---> [ Replica B (Ack) ]
                                                      ---> [ Replica C (Slow/Down) ]
   (Write Quorum W=2 satisfied; background read-repair heals Replica C)

sections.heading: Physical vs Logical Replication and Log Shipping
sections.body: Replicating database state between nodes relies on streaming changes recorded in the transaction log. Relational engines support two distinct mechanisms for keeping replicas in sync.
bullets: Physical Streaming Replication: Streams raw byte-level disk changes from the Write-Ahead Log (WAL). Extremely fast and exact bit-for-bit duplicate; downside is that both primary and replica must run identical operating systems and database binary versions.

Logical Replication: Decodes the WAL into row-level change events (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE). Allows replicating a subset of tables, streaming data across different database versions for zero-downtime upgrades, and feeding external event systems like Kafka via Change Data Capture (CDC).

Synchronous vs Asynchronous: Synchronous replication guarantees that at least one replica has written the change to disk before acknowledging the client (RPO = 0), but client write latency includes network round trips to the replica.

codeSnippet.title: PostgreSQL Synchronous Standby Configuration (postgresql.conf)
codeSnippet.code:
# Enforce that writes are acknowledged only after at least 1 replica confirms disk commit
synchronous_commit = on
synchronous_standby_names = 'FIRST 1 (replica_az2, replica_az3)'
# If primary fails, zero committed transactions are lost (RPO = 0)!

sections.heading: Failover Hazards, Split-Brain, and Promotion Lag
sections.body: Promoting a standby replica to primary when the active leader fails is one of the most fraught operations in distributed database infrastructure.
bullets: Split-Brain Risk: If a primary becomes unreachable due to a localized network partition, a standby may self-promote to primary while the old primary continues accepting writes. This produces divergent data that requires manual reconciliation.
Fencing Tokens: Ensure that when a new primary is elected, the old primary is isolated (STONITH: Shoot The Other Node In The Head) or rejected via fencing generation tokens.
Replication Lag during Failover: In asynchronous replication, promoting a replica that lagged by 50ms drops all writes committed to the primary during that 50ms window.

tradeOffs.pros: Zero data loss during failover (RPO = 0); replica is guaranteed to hold identical state.
tradeOffs.cons: Every write pays cross-node or cross-AZ network latency; a single stalled replica can halt all primary writes.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core banking ledgers, critical authentication state, and high-compliance financial platforms.

tradeOffs.pros: Minimal write latency on the primary; primary continues operating even if all replicas drop offline.
tradeOffs.cons: Replication lag can cause stale reads; risk of losing un-replicated transactions if the primary dies ungracefully.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-throughput read-heavy APIs, reporting databases, and cross-region disaster recovery standby nodes.

interviewTip: When discussing database failover, explicitly address the trade-off between RPO and write latency: 'We will use semi-synchronous replication where the primary waits for acknowledgment from one local replica across Availability Zones before returning success. This guarantees zero data loss (RPO = 0) without paying cross-region latency.'
